title: Building Patient, Unstoppable Attacks | Torre Attack & Alapin | GM Naroditsky's DYI Speedrun

moves.spoken: We face a knight to f3 and answer, of course, with a knight to f6.
White plays d4 — another King's Indian is coming.
We fianchetto with g6.
White plays c3 — a move with no independent value, the gateway to the London, the Torre, or a fianchetto setup.
We play a bishop to g7 and wait for White to show his cards.
A bishop to g5 — the Torre Attack, essentially a London but with the bishop on g5 instead of f4, which completely alters the character of the game.
We castle. Because the bishop is on g5, treating this like a London is innocuous for White.
Torre players usually go a knight to d2 and then either push e4 or play e3 — the ideas differ from the London, so keep them separate.
White plays the pawn to e3. The ideas in the Torre are very different from the London — don't treat this as a version of the London; from Black's side you need a separate set of ideas.
We keep the King's Indian spirit and push d6.

Now h4 — not a move I've faced, and it looks scary if you don't know it. Against h4 there are three options: ignore it and allow h5; push h5 ourselves to freeze the kingside; or push the pawn one square.
We choose the third — h6, encouraging White to hand us the bishop pair, then we push h5.
White captures on f6.
We recapture and White pushes h5.
And now the point of h6: we push g5, and the kingside is essentially frozen.
White plays a knight to d2. The drawback of what we did is the light squares.
We pushed h6, encouraged the trade, then h5 and g5 — what can bite us?
The light squares, in particular h7 — we must never allow White to build a battery on that diagonal, since a queen to h7 is no light threat.
One interesting move probably not on your radar: we push d5, restricting the knight and preventing it from jumping to e4.
A theme of these King's Indian games is flexibility — being a King's Indian player doesn't mean you can't play the move you think is best. I pushed d5 to restrict e4 and prepare an e5 break.
White plays a knight to h2, heading for g4.
A knight to g4 isn't scary, just annoying since it hits two pieces — so we bring the bishop back to g7.
White plays a queen to e2. Now we attack White's center — e5 wouldn't make sense here.
So we play the other break, c5 — because after e5, White just takes and we'd shuffle the bishop repeatedly.
White castles queenside — right into a massive attack. The queenside is never safe for White's king, but punishing it takes patience, not a hasty sacrifice.
A queen to a5 looks good, but the white king could evacuate to b1 and a1 — so first a bishop to f5, fixing the king on c1.
White plays a rook to e1. It's harder to shoot at a moving target — by fixing the king, we stop it fleeing to a1, and now a queen to a5 is much more effective.
A queen to a5 — mate is incoming very soon.
White plays a3. The immediate threat is a queen capture on a2.
We capture on d4 — not a bishop capture on d4, which is a blunder.
White recaptures on d4.
Patience is the crucial element — we set everything up by bringing the rook to c8, threatening a rook capture on c3.
The threatened rook capture on c3 leads to a quick mate: rook takes c3, the recapture, queen takes c3, king to d1, then a bishop check on c2 forces the king to e2, and a queen to d3 is mate.
We play the rook sacrifice on c3 with check.
White recaptures and we check with the queen on c3.
The king goes to d1 — the bishop to c2 is the key move.
A bishop check on c2 — if the king goes to c1, we play a bishop to d3 and a queen to c2.
The king is forced to e2 — a classic pattern to know.
And a queen to d3 is checkmate.
So c3, a bishop to g7 — if White plays a bishop to f4...
...we have a London.
Our opponent chose the Torre, so we start by castling.
White castles kingside.
The main line here is a knight to d2, preparing e4.
You play d6...
...and it turns out e4 is not scary in these positions.
But I like h6, asking the bishop where it's going.
Most people drop back to h4. One idea for your toolkit...
...if White captures on f6, how do you recapture?
Often in this structure the e-pawn recapture is strong, because you want to push f5.

After f5 you reopen the diagonal and chip at White's center — Black is doing great. An experienced Torre player puts the bishop on d3, but even there a knight to c6 preparing c5 keeps Black completely fine.
Black played f5, but the engine prefers c6, quietly controlling squares with f5 to follow — Black is completely fine either way.
A bishop to h4 is more common, since White doesn't want to give up the bishop.
And here remember that c5 is typically much better than e5 in the Torre.
You can orient toward the e5 break...
...but it's hard to get through with the bishop pinning the knight — an immediate e5 just blunders a pawn.
Preparing e5 with a knight to d7 is annoying because of the pin, and Black stays cramped.
c5 is a much better move. If White plays d5, then e6 gets rid of the pawn with free play; and if c4, then a rook to e8 collapses White's position, with the king stuck in the center.
The key point to remember: if White plays a knight to d2 and e4, throw in h6...
...then push c5, unafraid of d5.

You're not afraid of the captures on d5, the main line. White plays a bishop to c4, a knight to c6, and it's innocuous. Then the powerful knight to h5 leaves the h4 bishop with nowhere to go — the computer even prefers Black. A queen to c7 prevents the nasty e5, and a knight to a5 hits the other bishop.

Our opponent played the less ambitious e3 — nothing wrong, just unambitious. We proceed with d6, and h4 was already a novelty. We answered h6, forcing White's hand: after a bishop to f6, h5, g5, we have a great position. Then a knight to d2, d5, restricting e4.
